source: Positions from Lichess practice (lichess.org/practice). Explanations written for Chess Sathi.

checkmates.title: Checkmates
checkmates.blurb: Learn to finish the game: basic mates with a few pieces and the famous mating patterns.

fundamental-tactics.title: Fundamental tactics
fundamental-tactics.blurb: The everyday tricks that win pieces: pins, skewers, forks and more.

advanced-tactics.title: Advanced tactics
advanced-tactics.blurb: Deeper ideas strong players use: sacrifices, deflections and quiet killer moves.

pawn-endgames.title: Pawn endgames
pawn-endgames.blurb: When only kings and pawns are left, every tempo matters. Learn the key rules.

rook-endgames.title: Rook endgames
rook-endgames.blurb: The most common endgame in real games. Learn how to win them and how to save them.

topics.title: Piece Checkmates I
topics.intro: Checkmate a lonely king with a queen or a rook. Push the enemy king to the edge of the board step by step, then bring your own king close to help.

topics.title: Checkmate Patterns I
topics.intro: Common mating pictures, part 1. A king hiding behind its own pawns can be trapped on the back row. Spot the pattern and deliver the final blow.

topics.title: Checkmate Patterns II
topics.intro: More mating pictures. Look for squares around the enemy king that are blocked by its own pieces, then attack the last free square.

topics.title: Checkmate Patterns III
topics.intro: Mating patterns with teamwork: two pieces cover all the king's escape squares together. Find the pair of moves that closes the net.

topics.title: Checkmate Patterns IV
topics.intro: Advanced mating patterns, often with a sacrifice first. Give up material to rip open the king's shelter, then checkmate.

topics.title: Piece Checkmates II
topics.intro: Harder mates: a queen against a defending rook, bishop or knight, plus mating with two bishops and with knight and bishop. Take away squares patiently.

topics.title: Knight & Bishop Mate
topics.intro: The famous bishop-and-knight checkmate. You can only mate in a corner of the same colour as your bishop. Follow the method move by move.

topics.title: The Pin
topics.intro: A pin means a piece cannot move because something more valuable stands behind it. Pin a piece, then attack it again to win it.

topics.title: The Skewer
topics.intro: A skewer is a pin in reverse: attack a valuable piece, it moves away, and you capture the piece behind it.

topics.title: The Fork
topics.intro: A fork attacks two things at once. Your opponent can only save one of them. Knights are the best forkers, but every piece can fork.

topics.title: Discovered Attacks
topics.intro: Move one piece out of the way to uncover an attack from the piece behind it. Now you have two threats in one move.

topics.title: Double Check
topics.intro: A double check is a discovered attack where both pieces give check. The only answer is to move the king, which makes it very strong.

topics.title: Overloaded Pieces
topics.intro: An overloaded piece has too many jobs. Give it one more job and it can't do them all, so something falls.

topics.title: Zwischenzug
topics.intro: Zwischenzug means 'in-between move'. Before you recapture, look for a stronger move first, like a check or a bigger threat.

topics.title: X-Ray
topics.intro: An x-ray attack works through another piece. Your piece attacks or defends a square even though something stands in the way.

topics.title: Zugzwang
topics.intro: Zugzwang means any move your opponent makes will hurt them. Sometimes the best move is a quiet one that just waits.

topics.title: Interference
topics.intro: Interference means putting a piece between two enemy pieces so they can no longer protect each other.

topics.title: Greek Gift
topics.intro: The Greek gift sacrifice: give a bishop on h7 (or h2) to break open the castled king, then attack with knight and queen.

topics.title: Deflection
topics.intro: Deflection means forcing a defender away from the square or piece it protects. Lure it away, then strike.

topics.title: Attraction
topics.intro: Attraction means forcing the enemy king or a piece onto a bad square, usually with a sacrifice, then punishing it there.

topics.title: Underpromotion
topics.intro: Sometimes promoting to a queen is wrong. A knight, rook or bishop can give a fork or avoid stalemate.

topics.title: Desperado
topics.intro: A desperado is a piece that is lost anyway, so it grabs as much as it can before it goes.

topics.title: Counter Check
topics.intro: When you are in check, answer with a check of your own. A counter check can turn the tables.

topics.title: Undermining
topics.intro: Undermining means removing or attacking the piece that defends something important. Take away the guard and the target falls.

topics.title: Clearance
topics.intro: Clearance means moving your own piece out of the way, often with tempo, so another piece can use that square or line.

topics.title: Key Squares
topics.intro: Key squares: if your king reaches certain squares in front of your pawn, the pawn will promote no matter what.

chapters.name: Any key square by any route

topics.title: Opposition
topics.intro: The opposition: when two kings face each other with one square between them, the player who does not have to move is winning the fight.
